options.text: Conservative copying, where one new molecule keeps both original strands and the other is entirely new
options.misconception: describes conservative rather than semiconservative copying

options.text: Semiconservative copying, where every new molecule contains one old strand and one newly made strand

options.text: Random copying, where each new molecule takes strands from different original molecules by chance

questions.explanation: Semiconservative replication gives each daughter molecule one parental strand and one new strand, which is the old sheet plus new sheet picture. Option A describes conservative copying, and option C describes dispersive copying.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Unwinding the Duplex
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the duplex is opened for copying
questions.stem: A tram depot memo must explain why a document has to have its pages separated before duplication. Explain the equivalent step in DNA.

answer.exemplar: Before either strand can be copied the double helix has to be opened, and the enzyme helicase does this by breaking the hydrogen bonds between paired bases while single strand binding proteins hold the strands apart. The two separated strands then form a replication fork, and each exposed strand can serve as a template. A stable duplex cannot be read by the polymerase because the bases are paired inside it.

questions.explanation: The duplex must be unwound so both templates are exposed, and helicase separates the strands at the replication fork. Describing the polymerase as pulling the strands apart misplaces the job of helicase.
questions.hint: Name the enzyme that opens the duplex.

answer.exemplar: Compare the length of a chromosome before replication with the length in the daughter cells after one round of copying, using stained chromosomes, and then repeat for several rounds. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Antiparallel Strands and Direction of Synthesis
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the two new strands are made by different patterns
questions.stem: A planning memo on a new footbridge must explain why the two strands of a duplex are copied in different patterns. Explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: The two strands of the duplex are antiparallel, so they run in opposite 5 prime to 3 prime directions, but polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3 prime hydroxyl end. The strand that presents a 3 prime end towards the fork is therefore copied continuously as the leading strand, while the other is copied in short pieces away from the fork as Okazaki fragments, which are later joined.

questions.explanation: Because the strands are antiparallel but synthesis runs only 5 prime to 3 prime, one strand is made continuously and the other discontinuously in Okazaki fragments. Ignoring polarity misses why the patterns differ.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of each template.

questions.stem: A new hospital site memo must test whether an enzyme that separates the two strands of a duplex is required for copying. Design a test.

answer.exemplar: Compare cultures in which the separating enzyme is present with matched cultures in which its activity is blocked, and measure both the amount of new DNA made and the integrity of the copied DNA, alongside a control with no treatment. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The Semiconservative Outcome
questions.learningObjective: Explain what happens to the original strands during copying
questions.stem: A museum archive memo must explain why the original molecules are not all consumed during copying. Explain what happens to them.

answer.exemplar: Replication is semiconservative, so no original molecule is destroyed. When the duplex is opened, each parental strand becomes a template, and a new complementary strand is built alongside it, so every daughter molecule receives one original strand and one new one. Over many rounds the original strands are still present, each in a different molecule, and the number of new strands grows while the old ones are copied again.

questions.explanation: Because each parental strand is retained as a template rather than broken up, no original molecule is consumed during copying. Describing old strands as broken down and rebuilt misreads the semiconservative result.
questions.hint: Follow what happens to the parental strands.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Okazaki Fragments
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Okazaki fragments become one continuous strand
questions.stem: A rail depot memo must explain why short pieces of the new strand are later joined into one continuous strand. Explain the process.

answer.exemplar: The lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer, because the polymerase can only extend 5 prime to 3 prime and the template runs the other way. The primers are removed, the gaps are filled by a DNA polymerase using the free 3 prime end of the neighbouring fragment, and a ligase enzyme seals the remaining nick, producing one continuous daughter strand.

questions.explanation: Fragments are joined because each must be primed separately, and joining needs primer removal, gap filling and nick sealing by ligase. Leaving the fragments separate would leave the new strand discontinuous.
questions.hint: Primer removal, gap filling and sealing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The End Replication Problem
questions.learningObjective: Design a study showing that end shortening accumulates over rounds of copying
questions.stem: A greenway funding memo needs a study to show that the shortening seen in copied cells accumulates over successive rounds. Design the study.

answer.exemplar: Take cells from the same organism and measure the length of a chosen chromosome in freshly sampled cells, then in cells allowed one round of copying, then two rounds, then several more, using the same measurement method and the same chromosome each time. If the loss per round is constant and always occurs at the ends, the shortening accumulates linearly with the number of rounds, which is the signature of the end replication problem rather than random damage.

questions.explanation: To show accumulation you need successive rounds measured on the same chromosome with a constant method, and the loss must be at the ends rather than scattered. Random damage would not give the same small loss each round.
questions.hint: Measure the same chromosome over several rounds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Proofreading at the Growing End
questions.learningObjective: Explain how copying stays accurate over billions of added bases
questions.stem: Planning a new depot needs an explanation of accuracy during copying, so the memo must cover the safeguards. Explain them.

answer.exemplar: Accuracy rests on two mechanisms. Base pairing specificity means a polymerase usually inserts the complementary base, since the shape of the two purines and the two pyrimidines allow only sensible pairings. The proofreading activity then inspects the newest base pair at the 3 prime end, and if a mismatch is found the enzyme removes the wrong nucleotide, shifts back and resumes. Together these make the error rate roughly one in a billion added bases.

questions.explanation: Specificity of base pairing plus proofreading at the 3 prime end gives a very low error rate, because a mismatch can be removed before it becomes permanent. Base pairing alone is far less reliable.
questions.hint: Name both accuracy safeguards.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why separated strands must be held apart at the fork
questions.stem: A coastal path memo must explain why the separated strands must be held apart once the duplex has been opened. Explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: Once the two strands are separated each is a single stranded template, and these exposed stretches are chemically unstable and tend to fold back on themselves, pairing with their own complementary sequences and forming hairpin structures. Single strand binding proteins bind along the separated strands and hold them open, preventing that re-pairing so the polymerase can read along them. Without this, the fork would stall whenever a template folded back on itself.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the lagging strand needs many separate starting points

answer.exemplar: The lagging template runs in the direction that leaves the polymerase facing away from the fork, so if it tried to copy the whole strand in one pass it would be copying in the wrong direction. questions.topic: DNA Replication: Unwinding the Duplex
questions.learningObjective: Interpret evidence that strand separation is required for new DNA synthesis
questions.stem: A water treatment memo records that adding a compound that blocks a separating enzyme stops new DNA being made in a cell extract.

options.text: The compound must have damaged the template, so no new strand could be copied from it
options.misconception: blames template damage for the block

options.text: The compound stopped the duplex opening, so no template was available for copying
The compound must have stopped the nucleotides joining, because that step comes before unwinding
options.misconception: puts joining before unwinding

options.text: The compound must have filled the cell with sugar, so the building blocks were unavailable
options.misconception: invents sugar blocking of the reaction

questions.explanation: Blocking the enzyme that separates the strands means no exposed template exists, so no new strand can be made. Option C puts the joining step first, and option A blames damage to the template.
questions.hint: What does the blocked enzyme normally do?

questions.topic: DNA Replication: Antiparallel Strands and Direction of Synthesis
questions.learningObjective: Label the direction of growth on a template drawn 5 prime to 3 prime
questions.stem: A diagram in a cycleway memo draws one template 5 prime at the left and 3 prime at the right, with a polymerase on it and an arrow showing new DNA.

options.text: The arrow points left, because the polymerase always works back toward the 5 prime end
options.misconception: claims the polymerase works toward the 5 prime end

options.text: The arrow points right, because the new strand must match the template base by base
options.misconception: uses base matching to fix a direction

options.text: The arrow points left, because the new strand is built 5 prime to 3 prime from the primer's 3 prime end
The arrow points right, because the template is read from 3 prime to 5 prime
options.misconception: claims the template is read 3 prime to 5 prime

questions.explanation: New nucleotides are added to the 3 prime end, so on a template drawn 5 prime at the left the new strand grows leftwards. Option D misstates the direction of reading, and option A says the polymerase works toward the 5 prime end.
questions.hint: Add nucleotides to which end?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Time Needed to Copy a Genome
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the time needed to copy a specified genome length
questions.stem: The archive memo notes that a copied chromosome contains 3,600,000 base pairs and the enzyme adds 3,000 nucleotides each second. How many seconds does one strand take?
questions.explanation: 3,600,000 base pairs divided by 3,000 nucleotides per second is 1200 seconds. Multiplying the two numbers gives 10,800,000,000, and answering 3000 reports the rate rather than the time needed.
questions.hint: Divide the number of base pairs by the rate.
